report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not supported by the best available evidence. Taking ibuprofen does **not appear to worsen COVID-19 infection or outcomes**.

**Why the concern arose:** In March 2020, anecdotal reports and a public warning raised a hypothesis that ibuprofen and other NSAIDs might worsen COVID-19—partly through a proposed effect on ACE2, a cellular receptor involved in SARS‑CoV‑2 infection. This was biologically speculative, not clinical proof. WHO’s rapid review then found no direct evidence in patients with COVID‑19, SARS, or MERS; available information was indirect.  
https://www.who.int/news-room/commentaries/detail/the-use-of-non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs-(nsaids)-in-patients-with-covid-19

**What later evidence found:** Systematic reviews/meta-analyses of observational COVID-19 studies found no signal that NSAID use increased severe disease, hospitalization, or death. One 2022 review reported that, after adjustment for confounding factors, NSAID use was not associated with worse outcomes (and some analyses found lower severe-disease and mortality rates). These findings do **not** mean ibuprofen treats COVID-19; they mean the feared worsening effect was not observed.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9538204/  
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(22)00103-1/fulltext

The FDA likewise states it is not aware of scientific evidence linking NSAIDs such as ibuprofen to worsening COVID-19 symptoms.  
https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fda-advises-patients-use-non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs-nsaids-covid-19

**Practical caveat:** Ibuprofen still has ordinary risks—e.g., stomach bleeding/ulcers, kidney injury, cardiovascular risk, drug interactions, and avoidance in some pregnancies. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, follow the label, and ask a clinician/pharmacist if someone has kidney, heart, ulcer/bleeding disease, is dehydrated, or takes anticoagulants. It relieves fever/pain; it is not antiviral treatment.
